content: Pretraining Large Language Models Jingyuan Sun Lecturer of Natural Language Processing Department of Computer Science The University of Manchester Learning Outcomes Define LLM pretraining and explain why it is self-supervised.

Compare Transformer variants (encoder-only, encoder–decoder, decoder- only) and explain why modern LLMs use decoder-only with causal attention. Formulate the training objective: autoregressive probability factorisation, cross-entropy loss, and the difference between training vs inference.

Evaluate implications: limitations (e.g., hallucinations/bias), the impact of scale/compute, and how pretraining connects to adaptation and instruction tuning. Where We Are in the Pipeline Previously: – Transformers – BERT

– Training data for LLMs Today: – How large language models are pretrained Transformer Encoder Only Uses: NLU, classification, feature extraction Examples: BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa Encoder-Decoder Uses: NLG, translation, summarisation, seq2seq mapping Examples: T5, Flan-T5, BART Decoder Only Uses: NLG, translation, summarisation, completion Examples:

GPT-x, LLaMa, every other new model today Decoder-Only Architecture Modern LLMs: – Transformer decoder blocks – Causal attention (no access to future tokens) – Left-to-right generation Contrast with BERT: – Bidirectional – Masked LM GPT series Generative Pretrained Transformer series of models from OpenAI These are decoder transfer language models and can be used for generative tasks.
GPT (2018) GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) – Decoder-only – Pretrained on more data: WebText from Reddit (40GB) – Good at Generation Tasks GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020)

– Decoder-only – Pretrained on even more data (45TB) – Zero-Shot – One-Shot – Few-Shot Traditional Fine-Tuning GPT-3 ”In-Context” Learning Autoregressive Models and Self-supervised Learning Autoregressive Models – Naturally generative – Can produce long coherent text – Supports in-context learning Self-supervised Learning – No manual labels needed. – Training signal comes from: (1) text itself; (2) next-token prediction – This scales easily to massive datasets.
Why Decoder-Only? – Modern LLMs are predominantly decoder-only: GPT-4o Qwen3 Deepseek-R1 Llama4 – Efficiency Easier to scale and train – Strong Pretraining Excel in unsupervised pretraining

– Scalability Handles longer contexts and complex tasks What Is Pretraining? Pretraining: – Large-scale self-supervised training – Uses raw text (no human labels) – Learns general language modelling capability

Goal: Learn to model the probability of text. Language Modelling as Probability Estimation Goal of pretraining: Learn the probability distribution over text. Formally: Key idea: Model learns to predict each token given previous tokens. Autoregressive Objective Autoregressive training objective:

At each step: – See previous tokens (i.e. generation history) – Predict next token – Compute cross-entropy loss – Backpropagate gradients The model learns by minimising: Cross-entropy between predicted and true tokens. What Does This Mean Practically? Input: “The capital of France is [ ]”
Target: “Paris” The model learns by: – Predicting next tokens – Over trillions of examples Cross-Entropy Loss For each token: – yi= one-hot true token – pi= predicted probability

This penalises: Assigning low probability to correct token Intuition: Reward correct next-token predictions. Training vs Inference Training: – Predict next token – Compare with ground truth – Update weights Inference: – Predict next token – Sample or choose max

– Feed prediction back in Limitation of the Objective Since objective is purely predictive, the model may: – Hallucinate plausible but false information – Repeat biases in data – Generate unsafe content Fundamentally, it optimises the likelihood of text, not correctness or other properties.

Training Data Scale Typical scale: – Billions to trillions of tokens – Web text, books, code, Wikipedia Data preprocessing is important – Deduplication – Filtering – Quality control How large are “large” LMs?
Today, we mostly talk about two camps of models: – Medium-sized models: BERT/RoBERTa models (100M or 300M), T5 models – (220M, 770M, 3B) “Very” large LMs: models of 100+ billion

parameters Larger model sizes ⇒ larger compute, more expensive during inference Different sizes of LMs have different ways to adapt and use them – Fine-tuning, zero-shot/few-shot prompting, in-context learning… Emergent properties arise from model scale Trade-off between model size and corpus size Compute Requirements Training can involve:

– Thousands of GPUs / TPUs – Weeks to months of training – Distributed training Compute becomes the main constraint. Training vs inference cost – Training: expensive, done a few times (even once) – Inference:
cheaper, but many times Why LLMs The promise: one single model to solve many NLP tasks Emergent properties in LLMs Pre-training and adaption Pre-training: trained on huge

– amounts of unlabeled text using “self- – supervised” training objectives Adaptation: how to use a pre-trained model for your downstream task? – What types of NLP tasks (inputand output formats)? – How many annotated examples do you have? – Approach: Fine-tuning, Prompting, Instruction tuning
The Dominant Architecture of Transformer-based LLMs GPT-3: – Decoder-only Transformer – Causal attention – LayerNorm, residual blocks, etc. Modern LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, DeepSeek, etc.):

– Same core architecture – Sometimes improved normalization or efficiency – Minor architectural refinements – But the core is the same. Foundation vs Instruction Tuned Models Foundation ● Coherent, fluent generation ● Completion and continuation ● Vast world knowledge ● Potentially harmful outputs ● Difficult to control ● Misaligned with our values

Instruction Tuned ● Foundation ability and more ● Controllable by prompt ● Less need to fine-tune ● Follows any command ● Slight hit to performance ● Sensitive to prompt template Summary Pretraining – Large-scale self-supervised learning – Autoregressive next-token prediction – Trained on massive text corpora

What It Produces – Fluent text – World knowledge correlations – In-context learning capability – Generative foundation model What It does NOT Guarantee – Instruction following – Helpfulness or safety – Truthfulness
